title: About
text:
I’m a third-year Geomatics student at the University of Waterloo, with a minor in Computing. Geomatics brings together most of what I enjoy: computer science, geography, maps and data science.
I like making things, whether that’s code, a map, or a 3D view of a LiDAR point cloud, and I enjoy finding the visualization that makes a dataset click. Sometimes that extends to hardware, like building a GPS logger or writing sensor drivers for a Nordic Thingy:53, so I can collect the data myself.
Next, I want professional experience in remote sensing, especially RPAS, LiDAR and radar, and I’d love to work with geospatial data in less familiar terrain like the Arctic. I’m looking for co-op opportunities where I can build those skills on real-world, meaningful projects. My next co-op terms are back-to-back running from January 2027 to April 2027, and then from May 2027 to August 2027.

title: Geocoding 24 years of Kitchener building permits
text: New construction permits, 1999–2022, aggregated to a 0.25 km² hexagon grid.

title: Geocoding 24 years of Kitchener building permits
text:
Approach
The permit records had street addresses but no coordinates. I built an address locator from the city’s address-point layer, geocoded every permit, cleaned the results, and filtered to the “new construction” type. To make the patterns readable, I aggregated permits to a hexagonal grid and enabled time on the layer to animate it year by year.

I checked the unmatched addresses (for example, 2396 King St E) and found they point to locations in the middle of a road rather than a building. That’s why they’re missing from the city’s list of valid addresses: the problem is in the permit records, not the locator.

title: Geocoding 24 years of Kitchener building permits
text:
Results
New construction is concentrated on the edges of the city, in Trussler, Huron Park, Doon South, Williamsburg, Beechwood Forest and Grand River South. Those are the residential areas that grew during this period. A few cells near the core and along major roads pass 60 permits.

  




Permits issued per year.


Two peaks stand out: 2002–2007, during a period of strong residential growth, and 2014–2016, which lines up with ION light rail construction.

title: Geocoding 24 years of Kitchener building permits
text:
Limitations

Hexagon counts reflect how many addresses fall in each cell as well as how much building happened, so dense subdivisions score higher partly because they have more addresses. Normalising by address count would separate the two.
The link between the 2014–2016 peak and ION construction is a correlation I noticed, not something I tested.

title: Siting wind farms in Huron County
text: Suitability for wind turbines across Huron County with the baseline weights (5 = most suitable).

title: Siting wind farms in Huron County
text:
Approach
1. Build the factors. I clipped every layer to the county. For each constraint I created four buffer rings, starting from a minimum setback (for example, 550 m from buildings) and getting more suitable with distance. I then converted each to a raster on a shared 1–5 suitability scale. The Wind Atlas data had to be converted in QGIS before ArcGIS Pro could read it.
2. Weight and overlay. I combined the six factors in a weighted overlay:



Factor
Weight




Wind speed at 30 m
30 %


Distance from buildings
20 %


Distance from airports
15 %


Distance from urban areas
15 %


Distance from roads
10 %


Distance from wooded areas
10 %



Wind speed gets the most weight because without wind there’s no power. Buildings come next because they block wind and signal people nearby. Roads and woodland come last because they can be built around or cleared.
3. Test the weights. The weights are a judgement call, so I tested how much the answer depends on them. I reduced each factor’s weight in 10 % steps, from 90 % of its value down to 10 %, and redistributed the difference to the others. That gave 54 alternative suitability rasters. I then took the per-cell standard deviation across all 54 and classed cells with low variation (below 0.25) as stable.






Per-cell standard deviation across the 54 weight scenarios. Darker cells change less when the weights change.







Cells whose suitability stays stable under every weighting (green).

title: Siting wind farms in Huron County
text:
Result
A good site has to be both highly suitable with the baseline weights (class 4–5) and stable across the sensitivity runs. Large stable areas in the centre of the county were ruled out because they’re stable at only moderate or low suitability. Two areas pass both tests:






Site 1: northern and southern Ashfield-Colborne-Wawanosh.







Site 2: centre-west to north-west Bluewater, near the Lake Huron shore where wind speeds are highest.

title: Siting wind farms in Huron County
text:
Limitations

The 1–5 scores for each buffer ring are assumptions. A real study would base setbacks on Ontario’s renewable energy regulations and add constraints like protected areas and grid connection.
Wind Atlas data is a modelled long-term average at 30 m, below a modern turbine’s hub height.

title: GIS on a basketball court: shot accuracy maps
text: Kyle Lowry’s shooting percentage by court location, 2017–18 season.

title: GIS on a basketball court: shot accuracy maps
text:
Approach
Shot locations come in court coordinates, not latitude and longitude. I used a court image as the reference frame, plotted every shot as a point on it, and aggregated the shots into a hexagon grid. For each cell I calculated made ÷ attempted and classed it from 0–10 % up to over 75 %. The same workflow handles filtered subsets, such as one player or the team without that player.

title: GIS on a basketball court: shot accuracy maps
text:
Results






The 2017–18 Raptors as a team.







The Raptors without Lowry: almost identical to the full team.





Lowry was most accurate around the left, top and top-right of the three-point line, while the team as a whole was strongest just inside the arc. Removing Lowry barely changes the team map because his shots are a small share of the total.

title: GIS on a basketball court: shot accuracy maps
section: Comparing LeBron James vs Michael Jordan’s last game
text:
Comparing LeBron James vs Michael Jordan’s last game






LeBron James, 2022–23.







Michael Jordan, 2002–03 (his final season).





Both are highly accurate at the rim and in pockets of the mid-range. Jordan took far more mid-range shots, while James took more shots at or just behind the three-point line.

title: GIS on a basketball court: shot accuracy maps
text:
Limitations

Cells with only a handful of attempts can show 0 % or 100 % by chance. A minimum-attempts threshold, or shading by attempt count, would make the maps more honest.

title: Mapping police occurrences in Waterloo Region
text: Total 2023 occurrences in 0.5 km² hexagons, with an inset of the City of Waterloo.

title: Mapping police occurrences in Waterloo Region
text:
Approach
The occurrence CSV stored each location as one UTM “easting, northing” text field, which ArcGIS Pro can’t plot. I split it into separate coordinate columns, converted the records to points, and aggregated them to a 0.5 km² hexagon grid. I mapped total occurrences and individual types (assaults, fires and others) two ways: as a hexagon choropleth and as graduated symbols. Each map includes an inset of the City of Waterloo around the two universities and the college.

title: Mapping police occurrences in Waterloo Region
text:

title: Mapping police occurrences in Waterloo Region
text:
Results
Occurrences concentrate in the cores of Kitchener, Waterloo and Cambridge, with cells reaching several times the counts of the surrounding townships. Around the post-secondary campuses, activity clusters along University Avenue between Wilfrid Laurier and the east side of the University of Waterloo, the busiest stretch between the institutions.

title: Mapping police occurrences in Waterloo Region
text:
Limitations

These are raw counts. Because the cities hold most of the population, counts largely track where people are. Dividing by population or by daytime activity would show where occurrences are disproportionately high.
Recorded occurrences depend on reporting, so lower counts in rural areas partly reflect fewer people around to report incidents.

title: Where should the next fire station go?
text: Travel time of 10 minutes or less from the current stations plus both proposed sites, with recorded fire calls.

title: Where should the next fire station go?
text:
The question
In this scenario, the region is weighing two sites for a new fire station: New Hamburg in the west and Elmira in the north. I compared how each one would change response times and workload across the existing 16-station network.

title: Where should the next fire station go?
text:
Approach

Travel-time cost. I added a travel-time field to every road segment (length ÷ posted speed, in minutes) and built a network dataset with that cost and a one-way restriction.
Service areas. I generated 2-, 5- and 10-minute drive-time polygons for the current network, each proposed site on its own, and every combination.
Location-allocation. I assigned every recorded fire call to its nearest station by drive time under four scenarios (current, + New Hamburg, + Elmira, + both), then summarised average response time, calls left outside the 10-minute area, and calls per station.

title: Where should the next fire station go?
text:

On average response time and coverage the two sites are nearly tied. Each cuts the average by about 10 seconds and brings roughly 130 more calls inside the 10-minute area. The difference shows up on the map. Most calls near Elmira are already reached within 10 minutes by the existing network, and the region north of Elmira has very few calls. New Hamburg covers a cluster of calls on the western edge that the current network barely reaches, and it takes on 27 more calls than Elmira would.






New Hamburg on its own: the 10-minute area covers the western cluster of calls.







Elmira on its own: much of its area overlaps calls the existing network already reaches.





Recommendation: build at New Hamburg. It relieves more of the network, serves an area the current stations don’t reach quickly, and matches Elmira on average response time.



The current 16-station network for comparison.

title: Where should the next fire station go?
text:
Limitations

Travel times use posted speed limits with no turn penalties, traffic or emergency-vehicle behaviour, so absolute times are optimistic. The comparison between sites is more reliable than the minutes themselves.
The analysis uses one historical set of calls. A full siting study would also look at population growth and where calls are likely to come from in future.
